about.intro: I grew up in Dunmore Heath, studied business information systems at Eastbrook University and joined Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls in 2019, on the order desk next to Tilly Brandt, who taught me which orders really mattered. In 2021 I moved into sales operations, where Dennis Hale's spreadsheets became my reading list. In 2023 I became the Product Manager for Pinewick's online ordering. In 2025 I left to do an MBA at Marrowgate School of Management to deepen my grounding in finance and operations before my next PM role.
about.now: Writing teardowns on Sundays, playing second violin in a community orchestra and training for a faster half marathon.

suggested-routing-rules.context: Pinewick's online ordering lets offices, schools and clinics buy paper, toner and envelopes. Mid-size customers (20 to 100 staff) rarely planned ahead, so they ran out and phoned the sales desk for a rush delivery.
suggested-routing-rules.problem: Of 61,000 orders in 2023, 27% were rush orders: a phone call to Marla's desk, hand-keyed by Tilly, shipped on premium freight. Each added a median $38 in freight and left the dock re-planning its morning.
what_i_did: Pulled two years of order history and grouped it by customer, product and the gap between orders.
Interviewed 14 office managers. Most knew they ordered paper every few weeks but did not have time to set anything up.
Drafted the PRD for 'suggested standing orders': the site shows a customer a reorder it thinks is missing, the past orders behind it, and a single click to schedule it.
Paired with designers on the evidence card and with engineers on an overnight job rather than live scoring, which kept the cost down.

decisions.choice: Suggest standing orders instead of auto-reordering with a forecast model
decisions.why: Office managers said software should not spend their budget unseen. A reorder they approved themselves was one they could defend to accounts.
Brought the estimate down from two quarters to one, and customers plan supplies once a week at most.

results.note: 300 beta accounts against matched controls, 8 weeks

suggested-routing-rules.learned: ==Showing the evidence did more than making the suggestion.== Acceptance climbed from 29% to 47% once the card listed three past orders the standing order would have covered.
suggested-routing-rules.next: Extend suggestions to delivery windows, where customers make the same kind of last-minute calls.

slotwise.context: Pinewick's trade customers collect large print and paper orders from the loading dock. Pickups were arranged by phone, and Tilly Brandt answered the same questions every morning before the first coffee.
slotwise.problem: Tilly's desk took about 70 calls a day, and customers who never got through just turned up on Friday at four, when Wendell's two forklifts were already spoken for.
what_i_did: Spent four mornings at the front desk, noting down every call and how long it ran.
Put together a WhatsApp flow: the WhatsApp Business API through a booking tool, scheduling in a Google Sheet and reminders in Apps Script.
Added an evening-before reminder with a one-tap option to move the slot.
Ran it for ten weeks, meeting the dock crew each Friday to repair whatever had broken.

decisions.why: Every driver and buyer I spoke to already used it; nobody wanted to install anything to collect a box of envelopes.
Tilly could edit the schedule with no training, and Wendell could read it from the dock.

slotwise.learned: ==The nudge the night before beat the booking flow itself.== Missed pickups fell once customers could move a slot with one tap rather than phone in.
slotwise.next: Several customers asked to pay at pickup. A payment link in the reminder is the first thing I would test.

uc-reschedules.context: Brindlewood Courier delivers office supplies and print jobs across the Larchmont Falls valley. 12.0% of first delivery attempts failed, mostly because the front desk was empty or closed, and each failure cost a second van trip.
uc-reschedules.problem: Customers could not tell who was arriving or at what time. Many left the desk unattended because a four-hour window was too wide to plan around.
what_i_did: Listened to 40 recorded dispatcher calls and coded every reason a delivery failed.
Called 31 front-desk contacts whose delivery had failed in the last month.
Rode along with drivers for nine days, two of them full shifts, to see each route from the cab.
Designed a confirmation for the day before: driver photo, rating, a one-hour arrival window, and one tap for 'Confirm' or 'Change time'.
Ran the pilot with the depot in two zones alongside two control zones, with a Mixpanel funnel tracking confirmations and failures every day.

decisions.choice: One-hour arrival window, never a precise time
decisions.why: Drivers warned that a promised minute would be broken by traffic and cause more complaints.

decisions.choice: Send it at 5 pm rather than 8 pm
decisions.why: Customers who changed plans did so after 6 pm, so the message had to reach them before they logged off.
Failure rates swing with the day of the week, so comparing before with after would have fooled us.

uc-reschedules.learned: ==The driver's face beat the arrival window.== Receptionists told us a name and a photo made them plan to be at the desk, which explained many of the empty-desk failures.
uc-reschedules.next: Take it to two more depots with the same 5 pm send, and test whether keeping one driver per customer cuts failures further.
